title: Programming Language Forge
tagline: Languages as instruments, not identities — Python, Java, C++, and the systems beneath them.
blurb: IL-03 forges the programming backbone: Python, Java, and C++ taught as instruments with shared ideas (OOP, generics, streams, concurrency) compared across languages; data structures and algorithms as the single canonical node for the whole university; systems software from computer organization to software engineering; the MIT 6-3 course sequence as a reference layer; and a generative-art studio where code becomes visual craft. Original katas, bug zoos, race-condition laboratories, and cross-language exercises throughout — with Noah as Socratic debugging coach.

modules.title: The Programming Backbone: Python, Java, C++, DSA
modules.summary: Three languages as instruments — Python for fluency, Java for type-system discipline, C++ for memory honesty — plus the single canonical data-structures-and-algorithms node for the whole university: OOP, design patterns, functional programming, concurrency, and a bug zoo for testing and debugging with IDE and Git tooling.
objectives: Write idiomatic code in Python, Java, and C++, translating ideas across all three.
Implement arrays, lists, stacks, queues, trees, heaps, hash tables, and graphs; analyze sorting, divide-and-conquer, and dynamic programming.
Apply SOLID, the working set of design patterns, and refactoring with before/after discipline.
Write correct concurrent code: threads, virtual threads, async/await, locks — and reproduce races before fixing them.

notes.title: Python: fluency and the standard library
notes.body:
Python is the **first instrument**: syntax and control flow, functions and modules, OOP (classes, dunder methods, inheritance, dataclasses), and the standard library essentials (itertools, collections, pathlib, json, argparse, unittest).

- Idioms that matter: comprehensions, generators (lazy!), context managers, unpacking, f-strings
- The standard library is the language: reach for `collections.Counter`, `itertools.groupby`, `pathlib` before writing your own
- OOP in Python is protocol-oriented: duck typing, dunders (`__len__`, `__iter__`, `__enter__`), ABCs for interfaces
- Testing from day one: `unittest`/`pytest` basics, because the bug zoo (below) assumes you can write a failing test first

notes.title: Java: the type system as a teacher
notes.body:
Java teaches **discipline through types**: classes, inheritance, interfaces; generics with PECS; collections; streams and lambdas; virtual threads (Java 21).

- Generics: `? extends T` (producer — read) vs `? super T` (consumer — write). If you can't explain PECS, you don't know generics yet
- Streams are lazy: intermediate ops fuse and execute only at the terminal op — trace pipelines accordingly (see the IL-09 lab)
- Virtual threads: thread-per-task at massive scale for I/O-bound work; `synchronized` blocks pin carriers — prefer `ReentrantLock`
- The collections framework: know the Big-O of `ArrayList` vs `LinkedList` vs `HashMap` vs `TreeMap` operations — this is DSA made concrete

notes.title: C++: memory honesty
notes.body:
C++ teaches **what the machine actually does**: pointers and references, RAII, the STL, move semantics, build toolchains. It punishes imprecision — which is the lesson.

- RAII: resource acquisition is initialization — constructors acquire, destructors release; smart pointers (`unique_ptr`, `shared_ptr`) make ownership explicit
- Move semantics: `std::move` + rvalue references eliminate copies; the rule of five (or zero)
- The STL: containers, iterators, algorithms — `<algorithm>` is the most underused header in the language
- Undefined behavior drills: use-after-free, data races, signed overflow, uninitialized reads — learn to *predict* UB from reading code, because the compiler won't warn you twice
- Build toolchains: compile → link; headers vs translation units; CMake basics

notes.title: DSA: the canonical node
notes.body:
This is the **single canonical algorithms node** for the university (IL-08 deepens the theory; nothing is duplicated). Arrays, lists, stacks, queues; trees, heaps, hash tables; graphs (BFS/DFS, Dijkstra, topological sort); sorting (quicksort, mergesort, heapsort), divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming.

- Implement everything once by hand — then never again without reason; the implementation is the understanding
- Analysis: Big-O as a *comparative* tool (n log n vs n² at n=10⁶), best/average/worst cases, space-time trade-offs
- Dynamic programming: recognize optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems; memoization first, tabulation second
- Graphs: BFS for unweighted shortest path, Dijkstra for weighted (non-negative), union-find for connectivity
- Concurrency module: threads and races (produce the race in the lab, then fix it), virtual threads, Python async/await, locks and thread-safety — correctness before performance, always

cards.back: Laziness — they produce items on demand with O(1) memory, enabling infinite/large sequences and pipelined processing.
Producer Extends, Consumer Super: ? extends T when reading, ? super T when writing.

cards.front: Java streams: when does a filter execute?
cards.back: Only when a terminal operation runs — intermediate ops are lazy and fused per element.
Resource lifetime bound to object lifetime: constructor acquires, destructor releases — no leaks by construction.
If you define any of destructor, copy/move constructor, copy/move assignment — define (or delete) all five.
Non-negative edge weights. Negative weights need Bellman-Ford.
Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems → memoize first, tabulate second.
First reproduce the race in the sandbox, then fix it — a fix for a bug you can't reproduce is a guess.

quiz.q: What does this print? xs = [1,2,3]; it = (x*2 for x in xs); xs.append(4); print(list(it))
quiz.explain: Generators are lazy — the expression evaluates when consumed, seeing the appended 4.

quiz.q: Java: List<? super Integer> l — what can you add?
quiz.explain: Consumer super: safe to add Integer; the list holds Integer or a supertype.

quiz.q: C++: which is undefined behavior?
quiz.explain: Out-of-bounds write — classic UB; the compiler owes you nothing afterwards.

quiz.q: Best worst-case guarantee among quicksort/mergesort/heapsort?
quiz.explain: Heapsort is O(n log n) worst-case in-place; quicksort degrades to O(n²) without randomization.

quiz.q: BFS on an unweighted graph gives ___.
quiz.explain: BFS explores in increasing distance — first visit is via the fewest edges.

quiz.q: SOLID's 'D' (DIP) says ___.
quiz.explain: Dependency Inversion: high-level modules depend on abstractions — the seam that makes testing possible.

modules.title: Systems Software: Organization to Software Engineering
modules.summary: The substrate: computer organization (data representation, assembly, memory hierarchy, caching), operating systems (processes, scheduling, memory, filesystems), networks (TCP/IP, sockets, HTTP/DNS), databases and SQL, software engineering practice — then web fundamentals, API design, and the full-stack capstone that becomes portfolio evidence.
objectives: Explain data representation, the memory hierarchy, and caching performance effects.
Describe processes, scheduling, memory management, and filesystems as an OS designer would.
Write sockets code; debug networks with packet-level tools.
Design relational schemas, write complex SQL, and reason about transactions and indexes.
Ship a full-stack capstone: scoped, built, deployed, presented.

notes.title: Organization & OS: the machine's truth
notes.body:
**Computer organization**: bits → data representation (two's complement, IEEE 754), assembly basics (registers, the fetch-decode-execute cycle), the memory hierarchy (registers → L1/L2/L3 → RAM → SSD), and why caching dominates performance (locality: temporal + spatial).

**Operating systems**: processes vs threads, scheduling (FCFS, round-robin, priorities — and what starvation looks like), memory management (paging, virtual memory, TLB), filesystems (inodes, journaling).

- The cache exercise: traverse a matrix row-major vs column-major and *measure* — the 10x difference makes locality unforgettable
- Virtual memory: every process gets its own address space; the MMU + page tables maintain the illusion
- Cross-link: concepts become commands in IL-04's Linux path — learn the idea here, type it there

notes.title: Networks & databases: connection and persistence
notes.body:
**Networks**: TCP/IP and the OSI model as a troubleshooting map, sockets programming (TCP echo server → chat server), HTTP and DNS in depth, network debugging (ping, traceroute, dig, curl, packet capture reading).

**Databases**: the relational model, SQL (queries, joins, aggregation, subqueries), schema design and normalization (1NF–3NF, when to denormalize), transactions (ACID) and indexes (B-trees, what an index can and can't speed up).

- The sockets project series: blocking → select → threaded — feel the C10k problem before learning its solutions
- Normalization: eliminate redundancy via 3NF; denormalize deliberately for read performance, never by accident
- Index reasoning: indexes speed WHERE/JOIN/ORDER BY on the indexed columns; they cost on every write — design is trade-off
- Query gym: real database, graded query plans — EXPLAIN is the truth serum of SQL

notes.title: SWE, web, APIs, capstone
notes.body:
**Software engineering**: SDLC models (waterfall vs agile vs spiral — when each fits), requirements and design, testing strategies (unit/integration/e2e, the test pyramid), agile practice (standups, retros, backlog hygiene).

**Web fundamentals**: HTML/CSS, JavaScript in the browser (DOM, events, fetch), HTTP/REST/JSON, the frontend/backend connection.

**API design**: REST resource modeling, auth (sessions vs tokens vs OAuth shapes), versioning and contracts, documentation — contract-first exercises where your API is graded by a client you didn't write.

**Capstone**: project scoping (cut ruthlessly), full-stack implementation, deployment, portfolio presentation against a public rubric — the artifact that IL-10's career path presents as evidence.

cards.back: One representation for signed integers where addition 'just works' and there's a single zero.
Temporal: reuse the same data soon. Spatial: use nearby data soon. Caches exploit both.
Process: isolated address space. Thread: shared address space within a process — shared memory is the power and the peril.
Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — the transaction contract.
Every non-key attribute depends on the key, the whole key, and nothing but the key.
Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration, fewest slow e2e at the top.

quiz.q: Row-major vs column-major traversal on a large matrix: the lesson?
choices: cache locality — one can be ~10x faster
quiz.explain: Spatial locality: row-major matches C's layout — the cache-line effect is measurable and huge.

quiz.q: A page fault means ___.
choices: the MMU found no mapping — the OS must resolve it
quiz.explain: Page fault = address not currently mapped; the OS pages it in (or kills the process if invalid).

quiz.q: TCP vs UDP for a chat server: the real trade-off?
choices: TCP: reliability+ordering at latency cost; UDP: speed with app-managed reliability
quiz.explain: Choose by requirements: chat wants ordering (TCP); games/voice often take UDP + custom recovery.

quiz.q: Which normal form eliminates transitive dependencies?
quiz.explain: 3NF: non-key attributes depend only on the key — no transitive chains.

quiz.q: An index on (last_name) speeds up ___.
choices: WHERE last_name = ? and ORDER BY last_name
quiz.explain: Indexes serve lookups/sorts on their columns; they cost on writes and don't help unindexed scans.

quiz.q: Contract-first API exercise: who grades your API?
quiz.explain: Conformance tests from an independent client — the contract is the specification.

modules.title: MIT 6-3 Reference Layer
modules.summary: MIT's Electrical Engineering & Computer Science curriculum distilled in prerequisite order: 6.100A/B Python, 6.1200 Mathematics for Computer Science, 6.1210/6.1220 Algorithms, 6.1910 Computation Structures, 6.1800/6.1810 Systems and OS Engineering, 6.3900 Machine Learning. A reference layer — study schedules, problem-set trackers, and prerequisite gates — over MIT OpenCourseWare's public materials, with honest notes about term structure.
objectives: Sequence the 6-3 curriculum in prerequisite order with a personal study schedule.
Use the 6.100A/B problem sets as the Python practice spine.
Bridge 6.1200's discrete math into IL-02's canonical discrete node — no duplicated courses.
Gate the algorithms and ML nodes on verified prerequisites.

notes.title: 6.100A/B and 6.1200: the foundation pair
notes.body:
**6.100A/B (Introduction to Computer Science Programming in Python)**: the problem sets are the practice spine — do them in order, with Noah for Socratic help when stuck (hypothesis first, hints second).

**6.1200 (Mathematics for Computer Science)**: proofs and induction, number theory for CS, graph theory, probability for computing. This is the discrete-math bridge: where it overlaps IL-02's discrete module, the platform routes to the **single canonical node** — the global rule is no duplicated courses.

- Study schedule: one problem set per week per course is a full-time pace — plan accordingly
- Induction proofs: the template (base case, inductive hypothesis, inductive step) until it's muscle memory
- Number theory for CS: modular arithmetic, gcd, Fermat's little theorem — the RSA prerequisites

notes.title: 6.1210/6.1220 and 6.1910: algorithms and structures
notes.body:
**6.1210/6.1220 (Introduction to / Design and Analysis of Algorithms)**: sorting, hashing, divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming — with **prerequisite gating** against IL-02's discrete module (no induction fluency, no algorithms).

**6.1910 (Computation Structures)**: digital logic → the processor, assembly and the machine, caches and virtual memory, the hardware/software interface.

- Simulator-based labs for the digital-logic arc: build the ALU in the simulator before reading about pipelining
- The single canonical algorithms node is shared with Module 1's DSA — IL-08's theory track deepens it further
- Honest note: OCW problem sets assume the MIT term structure (recitations, office hours) — the study guide adapts the pacing for solo learners

notes.title: 6.1800/6.1810 and 6.3900: systems and the ML on-ramp
notes.body:
**6.1800 (Computer Systems Engineering)** + **6.1810 (Operating System Engineering)**: design principles at scale — the reading guide sequences the two courses' design papers (end-to-end argument, fate sharing, etc.), cross-linked to IL-04's hands-on Linux administration.

**6.3900 (Introduction to Machine Learning)**: ML principles and algorithms — with a **prerequisite audit**: the platform verifies IL-02's linear-algebra and probability nodes before opening this module, then routes the deep study to IL-07/IL-16.

- Read design papers actively: state the problem, the insight, the trade-off — one paragraph per paper
- The ML on-ramp is a *map*, not the territory: the territory is IL-07 (data/AI) and IL-16 (ML engineering)

cards.back: 6.100A/B Python → 6.1200 discrete math → 6.1210/1220 algorithms → 6.1910 computation structures → 6.1800/1810 systems → 6.3900 ML.

cards.front: Global rule when OCW overlaps IL-02?
cards.back: No duplicated courses — route to the single canonical node (IL-02's discrete module).
Prerequisite audit: IL-02 linear algebra + probability nodes verified first.
Base case → inductive hypothesis → inductive step. Muscle memory.
One paragraph per paper: the problem, the insight, the trade-off.

quiz.q: Why does the platform gate 6.1210 on discrete math?
choices: algorithms proofs need induction and asymptotics fluency
quiz.explain: Algorithm analysis is applied discrete math — without induction and Big-O fluency, the proofs are opaque.

quiz.q: 6.1910's arc in four steps?
quiz.explain: Computation Structures climbs from gates to the hardware/software interface.

quiz.q: The honest note about OCW problem sets?
choices: they assume MIT's term structure — pacing is adapted for solo learners
quiz.explain: Recitations and office hours don't exist for solo learners — the study guide re-paces accordingly.

quiz.q: Where does deep ML study live?
choices: IL-07 and IL-16 — 6.3900 is the on-ramp map
quiz.explain: 6.3900 maps the territory; IL-07 (data/AI) and IL-16 (ML engineering) are the territory.

modules.title: Generative Art: Circle Packing
modules.summary: The studio module: circle packing from first principles — rejection sampling, seeded randomness, Poisson-disc sampling, front-chain packing, spatial grids — then parameters as a design language (Span, Factor, NC, Alpha, AngleX/AngleY, blend modes), and the ethics of working from inspiration: attribution, inspired-by vs copied, lab notebooks, three studies.
objectives: Implement an honest rejection-sampling circle packer with a seeded RNG.
Upgrade to Poisson-disc and front-chain packing with spatial grids.
Read and write parameter blocks as design decisions.
Keep a lab notebook; attribute inspiration honestly; produce three studies.

notes.title: The packing problem, first principles
notes.body:
**Why circles**: they pack with visible tension — tangency reads as intention. **Rejection sampling**: propose a random candidate, reject if it collides, repeat — honest, simple, and slow enough to *feel* the algorithm.

- Seeded randomness: the same seed → the same piece. Reproducibility is the difference between art and accident
- Poisson-disc sampling: minimum-distance guarantees via the grid-accelerated dart-throwing algorithm — even coverage without clumping
- Front-chain packing: grow from the boundary inward, placing each circle tangent to the front — denser, more deliberate compositions
- Spatial grids: uniform-grid hashing makes collision checks O(1) amortized — the difference between a sketch and a system

notes.title: Parameters as a design language
notes.body:
Every parameter is a **design decision with a range**: **Span** (spacing — breathing room vs density), **Factor** (size falloff — hierarchy), **NC** (hue layers — palette depth), **Alpha** (opacity — atmosphere), **AngleX/AngleY** (field tilt — implied light/gravity), **blend modes** (how layers converse), **seeded variation** (controlled surprise).

- Read a parameter block like a score: each value is a choice about the piece's physics
- Change one parameter at a time; record the effect in the lab notebook — this is experimental method applied to aesthetics
- Blend modes are compositing math (multiply, screen, overlay) — know what the pixels do, not just what looks good

notes.title: Reading generative work: the ethics
notes.body:
**Attribution**: name the Pattlas piece (or any inspiration) explicitly — lineage is a feature. **Inspired-by vs copied**: same idea + your parameters + your notebook = inspired; same parameters + no transformation = copied.

- How to read any parameter block: reconstruct the artist's decisions — what did they fix, what did they vary, why
- Lab notebook practice: seed, parameters, intent, result, next experiment — every study gets an entry
- Three studies: same packer, three distinct parameter voices — breadth proves the instrument, not the accident

cards.back: Propose random candidates; reject on collision; repeat. Honest, simple, slow.
Same seed → same piece. Reproducibility separates art from accident.
Minimum distance between samples — even coverage, no clumping.
O(1) amortized collision checks via uniform-grid hashing.
Span = spacing (density). Factor = size falloff (hierarchy).
Same idea + your parameters + notebook = inspired. Same parameters, no transformation = copied.

quiz.q: Front-chain packing grows ___.
choices: from the boundary inward, tangent to the front
quiz.explain: Each new circle sits tangent to the existing front — denser, deliberate compositions.

quiz.q: Alpha controls ___.
quiz.explain: Alpha is opacity: the atmosphere and layering depth of the piece.

quiz.q: Your notebook entry must include ___.
choices: seed, parameters, intent, result, next experiment
quiz.explain: Seed + parameters + intent + result + next experiment — experimental method for aesthetics.

quiz.q: Using someone's exact parameter block with no transformation is ___.
quiz.explain: No transformation, no voice — that's copying. Attribute and transform.

scriptLabs.title: Lazy Pipeline: Generators vs Lists
scriptLabs.brief: Build a data pipeline two ways — list-based and generator-based — and measure peak memory on a large input. The required fragments force the laziness comparison.
scriptLabs.hint: Generator version: sum(x*x for x in range(n) if x % 2). tracemalloc.get_traced_memory()[1] is peak.

scriptLabs.title: Race Laboratory: Produce It, Then Fix It
scriptLabs.brief: Write a threaded counter increment that loses updates (the race), demonstrate the loss, then fix it with a lock. You must show the bug BEFORE the fix — a fix for an unreproduced bug is a guess.
scriptLabs.starter:
import threading

counter = 0

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        counter += 1  # race here

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print('expected 400000, got', counter)
# 1) run: observe the shortfall  2) fix with a lock  3) re-run: exact
scriptLabs.hint: Wrap the increment: lock = threading.Lock(); with lock: counter += 1. The with-block is the critical section.
scriptLabs.solution:
import threading

counter = 0
lock = threading.Lock()

def work():
    global counter
    for _ in range(100_000):
        with lock:          # critical section: read-modify-write is atomic now
            counter += 1

threads = [threading.Thread(target=work) for _ in range(4)]
[t.start() for t in threads]
[t.join() for t in threads]
print('expected 400000, got', counter)  # now exactly 400000
# Lesson: counter += 1 is three bytecodes (LOAD, ADD, STORE) — threads interleave between them.

scriptLabs.title: BST: Implement, Then Break, Then Balance-Talk
scriptLabs.brief: Implement a binary search tree with insert and inorder traversal. Then insert sorted data and observe the degeneration — the lab's point is feeling why balanced trees exist.
scriptLabs.hint: Height of degenerate sorted-insert tree = n-1. Inorder of a BST is always sorted — that's the invariant to test.

drills.title: Generics drill
drills.explain: PECS: Producer Extends — ? extends T for reading.

drills.title: Streams drill
drills.explain: Intermediate ops are lazy — execution happens at the terminal op (collect is one terminal op).

drills.title: RAII drill
drills.explain: Constructor acquires, destructor releases — scoped, deterministic, exception-safe.

drills.title: Big-O drill
drills.prompt: Binary search on n=1M sorted items: ~comparisons?
drills.explain: log2(1M) ≈ 20 — the power of logarithmic search.

drills.title: Transactions drill
drills.explain: Isolation — concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work.

drills.title: API drill
choices: PUT idempotent (same effect repeated); POST not necessarily
drills.explain: PUT replaces the resource state — repeating it converges; POST typically creates anew.

scenarios.title: Choosing the Language for the Job
scenarios.context: You need: a CLI tool parsing 10GB of logs fast, and a web dashboard for the results. One language or two?

options.text: C++ or Rust-class systems language — throughput is the requirement
options.why: 10GB parsing is throughput-bound; zero-cost abstraction and memory control win. Python would work but 10-50x slower.
Write-speed doesn't matter if runtime misses the SLA — and the dashboard needs the data on time.

options.text: Python (Flask/FastAPI) or JS — ecosystem speed for CRUD + charts
options.why: Dashboards are I/O-bound glue — the ecosystem (ORMs, chart libs, auth) matters more than raw speed.
Possible, miserable: you'd hand-roll what web frameworks give for free. Instruments, not identities.

scenarios.title: The Slow Query
scenarios.context: A dashboard query on orders (10M rows) takes 14s. EXPLAIN shows a full table scan on WHERE customer_id = ? AND status = ?.

options.text: Add a composite index on (customer_id, status)
options.why: The query filters on both columns — a composite index serves the WHERE directly. Verify with EXPLAIN after.

options.text: Add more RAM to the database server
options.why: Hardware masks the problem at 10M rows and bankrupts you at 100M. Fix the access path first.

options.text: Cache the whole table in Redis
options.why: Caching helps repeated identical queries but the scan still happens on miss — and invalidation becomes your new problem.

steps.prompt: After the index, it's 40ms. What do you document?

options.text: The index definition, the before/after EXPLAIN, and the write-cost trade-off
options.why: Indexes cost on every write — the decision record lets the next engineer reason about it.
Undocumented performance fixes get reverted by the next migration. The lab notebook habit applies to production too.

trainers.title: Big-O Sprint Trainer
trainers.brief: Rapid-fire complexity identification: random code snippets, name the Big-O. Streak-tracked — analysis speed is an interview survival skill.

terminalSims.title: Git Rescue Simulator
terminalSims.brief: Canned git scenarios: detached HEAD, merge conflict markers, accidental commit to main. Exact-match commands with fuzzy 'did you mean' — practice the rescue before you need it.

mockTasks.explain: Laziness — items produced on demand, constant memory.
Consumer Super — safe to write T into the collection.
Ownership semantics: unique_ptr is exclusive and movable; shared_ptr shares via refcount.

mockTasks.q: Quicksort worst case and the fix?
choices: O(n²) on sorted input; randomize the pivot
mockTasks.explain: Sorted input + first-element pivot = degenerate; randomization restores expected O(n log n).
Negative weights break the greedy invariant — use Bellman-Ford.

mockTasks.q: counter += 1 across threads loses updates because ___.
mockTasks.explain: LOAD/ADD/STORE interleave — the lock makes the trio atomic.

mockTasks.q: Row-major vs column-major in C: the lesson?
mockTasks.explain: C is row-major; matching traversal exploits cache lines.
Non-key attributes depend on the key, the whole key, nothing but the key.
PUT (and DELETE) converge on repeat; POST typically creates anew.
Minimum distance — even coverage without clumping.
Span = spacing — the breathing room of the composition.
Proofs, number theory, graphs, probability — the math CS runs on.

mockTasks.prompt: Write a Python generator yielding squares of even numbers below n.
mockTasks.explain: Lazy generator: filter evens, yield squares — O(1) memory.

mockTasks.prompt: SQL: customers with no orders over $100 (keep all customers).
mockTasks.starter:
-- customers(id,name), orders(id,customer_id,total)
SELECT c.name
FROM customers c
-- complete the join
mockTasks.answer: SELECT c.name FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.total > 100 WHERE o.id IS NULL;
mockTasks.explain: Filter in ON preserves the outer join; WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps only customers with no big orders.

answerBank.q: Which language should I learn first?
answerBank.a: Python — fastest to fluency, gentlest error messages, largest library. Then Java for type discipline, then C++ for the memory model. The order is pedagogical, not tribal.

answerBank.q: How do I actually get good at DSA?
answerBank.a: Implement every structure once by hand, analyze every algorithm's complexity, then do timed problems. The implementation is the understanding; the analysis is the interview skill. IL-08 deepens the theory later.

answerBank.q: Java streams confuse me — where do I start?
answerBank.a: Internalize laziness first: intermediate ops (filter/map/peek) do nothing until a terminal op (collect/forEach) runs. Trace the IL-09 stream lab by hand, annotating LAZY vs TERMINAL per line.

If you touch systems, games, embedded, high-frequency, or browsers — yes. Otherwise, learn enough to read it: RAII, pointers vs references, and why UB is the exam's favorite trap. The memory honesty transfers everywhere.

answerBank.q: How do MIT OCW courses fit a solo learner?
answerBank.a: Use the 6-3 sequence as a reading/study guide with the adapted pacing in Module 3 — one problem set per week per course is full-time pace. Verify prerequisites (discrete math before algorithms) via the gates.

It's algorithms with aesthetic output: sampling theory, spatial data structures, experimental method. The studio trains precision (parameters as decisions) and documentation (lab notebooks) — both production skills.
